materials.title: DND scenes Rubric
materials.content:
Plot  (story)  %30

Does the scene have all the elements of a story arc?

 

Exposition



Moment of incidence



Sequence of events



Climax



Resolution



Character (performance) %30

Are characters defined, recognizable, and well portrayed? (unity of character)



Do characters serve a purpose in the story?  (Protagonists, antagonists, supporting, ensemble, etc.)



Do actors embody their characters?



Are the actors believable? Do they stay in character?

 

 

Thought %10

What themes go along with the story? 

 

What are the elements of fantasy in the story?

 

What’s the idea behind the scene?

 

Diction %20

Does the diction move the story along?

What does the diction show and what does the diction tell?

 

 

Is the Diction stylized? Does it match the fantasy theme? (avoid modern dialogue, lean towards dialogue from high fantasy books, video games, comics, and other similar media)




Music / Spectacle %10

Does the story flow? What is the pacing? 

 

How long is the scene (7-10 minutes expected)

 

What staging choices are made? (stage composition / set)

 

 

What costumes / props are used? Do they contribute to the story?

 

What does the lighting look like? (you may have up to 4 light cues)

 

Do the sound cues / scoring serve a purpose? (may use up to 4 sound cues and one underscoring song)

children.title: DND Character Development project

assignmentDetails.description:
Character Development with D&D Species

Objective:
In this assignment, you will develop a unique character based on a randomly chosen Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) species. The focus is on deepening your understanding of character creation, focusing on the components of a character’s background and personality using Aristotle’s Poetics. You will explore character traits, physical characteristics, and a backstory, and how those elements can influence a character’s actions, motivations, and decisions in a story.

 

Answer the following prompts and questions. 

  1. Randomly Assigned Species:
    You will be randomly assigned a D&D species (such as Elf, Dwarf, Tiefling, etc.). This will serve as the foundation for your character and will influence your build and backstory. Yyou will not be playing this character in a game. Don't worry about the character stats or nitty gritty details (example: ability checks, AC, and pretty much any numbers you see)

  2. Choose a Class: In DND, a class is more than a job; it's a life calling that can can be influenced by your whole personality, background, style, and character journey!

  3. Character Details (Personality and Traits):

    • Name: Choose a name for your character. Be creative, and think about how your character’s name might reflect their background or culture.
    • Personality Traits: Write about your character’s ethical nature, attitude, and sense of self. Think about how they approach life and their interactions with others. Do they trust easily? Are they brave, cautious, kind, or cunning? List 5 personality traits
    • Allignment: Refer to the allignment page 
    • Strengths and Weaknesses: What is your character good at? What are their flaws or vulnerabilities? These will make them more dynamic. list 3 strengths and 3 weaknesses
      • Example: A strong fighter might be overconfident, or a compassionate healer might be too trusting.
    • Motivations: What does your character want most in life? What are they striving for? How does this tie into their strengths, weaknesses, and personality traits? This will probably tie into your backstory. 1 or 2 sentences for this one.

  4. Physical Characteristics:

    • Appearance: Describe what your character looks like. Focus on key physical features such as:
      • Height, build, and posture.
      • Unique features (e.g., color of skin, eyes, hair, fur, or scales).
      • Distinctive markings, scars, or tattoos.
      • Facial expressions that reflect their personality (e.g., do they smile often or have a serious demeanor?).
    • Body Language: How do they carry themselves? How do they move, stand, or react to different situations? Are they quick and agile or slow and deliberate?

  5. Backstory:

    • Origin Story: Where does your character come from? What is their cultural background and how has it shaped them? Write a complete paragraph for this origin story.
    • Key Life Events: What are some defining moments in their past that influenced who they are today? Think about both positive and negative events that shaped their personality and choices.
      • Example: Were they orphaned and had to fend for themselves? Did they experience a great loss or victory?
    • Conflict/Goal: What does your character want or need? What’s standing in their way? Think of how their backstory can create internal or external conflict that drives them forward in a story.

  6. Character Rendering

    • Visual Representation: You can create a visual representation of your character using drawing, an online tool like Kleki, or HeroForge. Submit this to the seperate assignment "Character Rendering"
      • If you choose to draw your character, focus on illustrating key features you described in your character’s appearance. This helps you visualize them more fully and enhances your understanding of their personality and background.

 

Guidelines for Reflection: As you create your character, think about how they fit into a larger story. Consider how their personality and history will influence their actions and relationships with others. Focus on the following elements from Aristotle’s Poetics to guide your thinking:

  • Character: What makes your character unique, and how does their personality shape their decisions and relationships with others in the story?
  • Motivation: Why does your character do what they do? What drives them forward?
  • Consistency: Is your character’s behavior consistent throughout their story? Does their behavior change, and if so, why?
  • Catharsis: How might your character’s journey evoke an emotional response from an audience? Does their growth, struggle, or failure move people?

Rubric:

  • Character Depth: Come up with personality traits, physical characteristics, and a well-developed and believable backstory. 
  • Creativity: How original and unique is the character design and backstory? Did you think outside the box when developing your character?
  • Visual Representation : Does the character’s visual rendering reflect their personality and backstory in a meaningful way?

Good luck, and remember to have fun exploring the depths of your character’s mind and background! The more creative and detailed you get, the more you’ll understand how to bring compelling characters to life in stories.

children.title: The Yellow Boat Post Read through questions

assignmentDetails.description:
Answer each question in complete sentences and use thorough detail. This is a more in depth journal entry than we've had all year; you're going to want to put in a sincere effort and dedicate some time to reflect on this story. This is also the last journal entry of the nine weeks, so if you do the math for grade calculations, an incomplete grade on this homework will really dent your grade!!

Huge tip: I encourage you to look back at the play as you complete your analysis. 

 

Story Analysis

1. in a complete paragraph, summarize David Saar's The Yellow Boat. Be sure to mention the elements of the story arc (exposition, moment of incidence, rising action, etc. )

2. Benjamin's characterization: what is Benjamin like? How would you define his character objectives in this play? (remember: all characters have motives, objectives, obstacles, and strategies in their own story)

3. What are Ben's parents like? What kind of family dynamics do they have with Benjamin?

4. Think about a few of the named characters played by the ensemble in the play. What role do they serve in Benjamin's Story? Name three characters, describe them, and talk about what they represent to Benjamin.

5. This play relies on an ensemble to build the different settings Benjamin finds himself in, creating an envornmental effect for Ben's school, community, and the world around him. List three of the groups the ensemble portrays in the show. 

Play Structure Analysis

5. This Play is told from the perspective and imaginative world of Benjamin. How does this affect how the characters act and speak?

6. In the preface of the show, the playwrite tells us that in this show, time is not linear. What does "cinematic time" mean, and how does that affect the flow of the play?

7. Benjamin is very creative, loves to draw, and loves to play! How does Benjamin use colors (literally and metaphorically) in the show? 

8. What purpose does the Yellow Boat serve in the story, both as a set piece, and an extended metaphor throughout the show?

Reflection

9. What were your favorite parts of this play? What made you laugh? What scenes were cool or interesting in your imagination during our read through? How did you feel from the start of the readthrough to the end of it?

10. What are your final takeaways from The Yellow Boat?

children.title: Story Adaption: The Bamboo Cutter
children.content:
Students will read the Japanese fairy tale, The Bamboo Cutter. They will mark the elements of this story's narrative arc: Exposition, Moment of incidence, Rising action, Climax, and Resolution that follows. 

Students will then be split into groups and begin adapting the story into a 5-7 minute performance that will be performed in front of the class. A brief analysis and justification of the group's adaption done individually up with will also be due in paragraph form.

 

Part One - As a Group, discuss the important moments of the story and brainstorm how to turn it into a show.

Part Two  - Create the story arc (beginning, middle, and end) of the ritual, write it down, brainstorm.

-Collaborate to establish team members theatrical roles in the performance. Everyone has a place at the table, and everyone has a voice. You are graded in part by your ability to work well with others. 

-Incorporate symbolism into your story and justify its use.

-Choreograph dynamic beats. Be specific!!

-Utilize body and movement to create a soundscape (the music and sounds of the world). You may use the lamp as a lighting practical if desired.

-At this time, brainstorm what costumes, props, mask decorations you’d like to use. 

Part Three - Rehearse and choreograph as a group: create stage pictures evocative of the story you aim to collectively tell. Incorporate levels and variations of movement, using your full acting instrument to story tell. 

Part Four - Design masks using paper plates and decorations, find costumes and props, and rehearse up to a performance ready level.

Part Five - final performance, class debrief and teacher notes, Post performance written analysis to follow.

Go for mood based music for the scoring. What's the vibe of the scene, and what music fits the vibe?

This is due Wednesday, 1/22

This performance grade is a participation grade based on your experience rehearsing and performing in our Cinderella production.

Your exit ticket is a hand written "letter to yourself" that you will seal in an envelope and open at the end of the year. This is meant to be a reflective journal on the past month or so of working with this script, your character(s), this cast, and this class. I will not view what you write. This is for you to gather your thoughts and feelings, put them away, and open them up at the end of the year! You can make this whatever you want, but I encourage you to make it something that will be meaningful to you!

 

Turn this in to me by Friday during class. I'll provide envelopes.

1. Choose one of your poems you devised for class ( Passion, Loss, or Ignorance) and revise it. The goal of this revision is to expand on the ideas, metaphors, personal anecdotes, or word play you used in your chosen poem. Get more specific, find different perspectives, and craft a story that amplifies your voice! I want these poems to be at least two minutes in length Were you to read your poem aloud.

2. Write a brief pargraph explanating why you chose this poem to work with, and the inspiration you found while working on it / revising it.

 

To upload, ether post your poem in the Create tab of this assignment, or upload a picture of your revised poem if you prefer to hand write it. We will present these poems in class on Monday (2/24): I'll check to see if you've uploaded the poem that morning. 10 points off per day missing.

Grading Scale: 80% completion, 20% revised content.
